posts.headline: 3 Concerts in 12 Days
posts.prose: I don't know what got into me in July 2023, but I saw 3 shows across 3 different genres in 12 days without once feeling like I was overdoing it. Foals at The Belasco on the 18th, UB40 at Peacock Theater on the 21st, X at Pacific Amphitheatre in Costa Mesa on the 30th — indie rock, reggae, and punk, all inside a single Los Angeles summer. There's something about that stretch that still makes me smile: I went from the close, sweaty energy of The Belasco to an amphitheatre in Orange County without stopping to ask whether any of it made sense as a playlist. It didn't, and that was exactly the point.

social.hook: Indie rock, reggae, and punk — 3 shows, 3 genres, 12 days.
social.caption: Foals at The Belasco on the 18th, UB40 at Peacock Theater on the 21st, X at Pacific Amphitheatre on the 30th. One Los Angeles summer, no attempt to make it a coherent playlist.
beats: July 2023: three shows in twelve days across three genres I would never put on the same playlist.
Foals at The Belasco on the 18th — close, sweaty, the room doing exactly what a room that size should do.
UB40 at Peacock Theater on the 21st, then X at Pacific Amphitheatre in Costa Mesa nine days after the first show.
Indie rock to reggae to punk without stopping to ask whether any of it made sense. It didn't, and that was the point.

posts.headline: Social Distortion — 1.4 Years Before Born to Kill
posts.prose: Punk rock has always been about the song before the studio catches up, and at The Belasco in Los Angeles on December 6, 2024, I heard four tracks from *Born to Kill* a full 518 days before the record existed in anyone's hands. Four songs — "Tonight," "Over You," "The Way Things Were," and the title track itself — dropped into an 18-song set like they'd always belonged there, which, knowing Social Distortion, they probably had for years already. That's the thing about a band formed in 1979: they don't audition new material, they road-test it, and the crowd at The Belasco had no idea they were the test.

social.hook: Four songs from an album that wouldn't exist for 518 more days.
social.caption: Social Distortion road-tested 'Tonight,' 'Over You,' 'The Way Things Were,' and 'Born to Kill' at The Belasco on December 6, 2024. The crowd had no idea they were the test.
beats: An 18-song set at The Belasco — and four of them hadn't been recorded yet.
'Tonight,' 'Over You,' 'The Way Things Were,' and 'Born to Kill' dropped in like they'd always been there.
They had, probably. A band formed in 1979 doesn't audition new material — it road-tests it.
518 days before Born to Kill existed in anyone's hands, Los Angeles heard it first.

posts.headline: "Notorious": Nile Rodgers and Duran Duran, 39 Years Apart
posts.prose: "Notorious" is a song with two authors in a sense — Duran Duran wrote it, but Nile Rodgers produced it, and his fingerprints are all over that bassline. I heard Duran Duran play it at Irvine Meadows in July 1987, and then 39 years later I watched Rodgers claim it fully at the Pacific Amphitheatre, playing it as his own with complete justification. Two different Southern California venues, two different summers, the same song landing with the same authority both times. I didn't plan that symmetry — it just accumulated in my ticket stubs, waiting for me to notice.

social.hook: 39 years between ticket stubs, same song, same authority
social.caption: Duran Duran wrote 'Notorious'; Nile Rodgers produced it. I heard them play it at Irvine Meadows in 1987, then watched him take it back thirty-nine years later.
beats: Duran Duran wrote 'Notorious.' Nile Rodgers produced it — and his fingerprints are all over that bassline.
I heard Duran Duran play it at Irvine Meadows, July 1987. Southern California, summer, the song brand new.
Thirty-nine years later, Rodgers played it at Pacific Amphitheatre as his own — with complete justification.
Two venues, two summers, the same song landing with the same authority both times.
I didn't plan that symmetry. It just accumulated in my ticket stubs, waiting for me to notice.

posts.headline: July 31: 40 Years Since The Art of Noise
posts.prose: I drove down to the Pacific Amphitheatre in Costa Mesa on July 31, 1986, genuinely unsure what a live Art of Noise show would even look like — they were a studio project, built from samples and synthesizers, and the stage setup felt more like a science experiment than a concert. It's been 40 years since that night, and I still remember the disorientation of watching music that seemed to exist only on record suddenly fill an outdoor amphitheatre with actual air and heat and crowd noise. They had already released *(Who's Afraid of) The Art of Noise?* by then, and hearing those fractured rhythms in the open California summer felt genuinely strange in the best way. Some shows you attend; that one attended me.

audio.albumName: And What Have You Done With My Body, God?

social.hook: A studio project made of samples — and somehow it filled the open air.
social.caption: Art of Noise were built in a studio from samples and synthesizers, not designed for a stage. I drove to the Pacific Amphitheatre in 1986 and watched them prove that wrong.
beats: July 31, 1986. I drove to Costa Mesa genuinely unsure what I was about to see.
Art of Noise were a studio project — samples, synthesizers, no obvious band to watch.
The stage setup looked like a science experiment. Then the fractured rhythms hit the open California air.
(Who's Afraid of) The Art of Noise? was already out. Hearing it live felt strange in the best way.
Some shows you attend. That one attended me.

posts.headline: Pacific Amphitheatre: 16 Shows Over 5 Decades
posts.prose: I was 16 years old the first time I walked into the Pacific Amphitheatre, catching Tears For Fears in the summer of 1985 — right in the thick of the *Songs from the Big Chair* era. Thirty-nine years later, I closed the loop with The English Beat in July 2024, and somewhere in between I fit in 14 more nights at that Costa Mesa bowl, from the Beach Boys to Run-DMC to UB40. Sixteen shows across 5 decades at the same venue feels less like a habit and more like a relationship. I didn't plan any of this, which somehow makes it better.

audio.trackName: Everybody Wants to Rule the World

social.hook: Pacific Amphitheatre got me at 16. It took 39 more years to finish what that started.
social.caption: I walked into Pacific Amphitheatre for the first time in 1985 for Tears For Fears, mid-Songs from the Big Chair. The English Beat closed it out in July 2024 — 16 shows I never once planned.
beats: Summer 1985. I was 16, Tears For Fears were everywhere, and Pacific Amphitheatre was a revelation.
Fourteen more nights followed: Beach Boys, Run-DMC, Sting, Garbage, UB40, Yazoo — the list kept growing.
Five decades of shows at one Costa Mesa bowl, and I never sat down and decided to make it a thing.
The English Beat in July 2024 turned out to be show sixteen. I only knew that after I counted.
Not a plan. Not a project. Just a place that kept being the right answer for 39 years.

posts.headline: July 16: 40 Years Since Beach Boys
posts.prose: I was at the Pacific Amphitheatre in Costa Mesa on July 16, 1986 — 40 years ago today — and I still remember the way the summer air felt when the opening notes hit. The Beach Boys had been together 25 years by then, and somehow they made those harmonies sound like they were being invented right there in front of me. It was one of my earliest entries in what would become decades of concert-going, and I had no idea I was starting something. Forty years later, that night still feels like the right place to have begun.

audio.albumName: The Very Best of The Beach Boys: Sounds of Summer

social.hook: I had no idea I was starting something.
social.caption: The Beach Boys were 25 years into those harmonies when I heard them at Pacific Amphitheatre in 1986. One of my earliest entries in what became four decades of concert-going.
beats: July 16, 1986: one of my earliest concert entries, though I didn't know it yet.
The Beach Boys were already 25 years together — and the harmonies sounded like they were being invented on the spot.
Pacific Amphitheatre, summer air, opening notes. The right place to have begun, as it turned out.
Forty years on, that night still sits near the top of the archive — not for what it was, but for what it started.

posts.headline: House of Blues Anaheim: 6 Shows Over 3 Decades
posts.prose: I still think about walking into House of Blues Anaheim for the first time in August 2003 to see Joe Jackson — an artist who'd been making records since before I probably knew what a record was. Six shows across three decades at that same room, from that night with Joe Jackson all the way to Social Distortion in December 2022, with Streetlight Manifesto, Future Islands, and Royal Blood filling the years in between. Five artists who share almost nothing sonically, which tells me the venue was doing something right. Somehow a club in Anaheim became a quiet constant in my concert life, and I never quite planned it that way.

social.hook: House of Blues Anaheim kept showing up in my life. I never once booked it on purpose.
social.caption: Six shows at House of Blues Anaheim, five artists with nothing in common sonically. Joe Jackson opened it in 2003; Social Distortion closed it in 2022. The room did the choosing.
beats: August 2003: Joe Jackson at House of Blues Anaheim. That was the night the room got its hooks in me.
Streetlight Manifesto, Future Islands, Royal Blood, Social Distortion — five artists who share almost no sonic DNA.
A club in Anaheim, six shows across three decades, and I never once sat down and planned any of it.
The through-line wasn't genre or era. It was the room itself, quietly doing something right.

posts.headline: Ziggy Marley: Caught Once, Never Again
posts.prose: One show in 36 years of concert-going — just Ziggy Marley, Mesa Amphitheatre, September 1988, and then nothing. I've seen artists dozens of times, built whole chapters of this archive around them, but somehow Ziggy never crossed my path again despite releasing records like *Rebellion Rises* and *Love Is My Religion* that I genuinely love. That single 1988 date sits in the archive like a polaroid found in a jacket pocket — vivid, a little mysterious, and making me wonder how I let 36 years slip by without a second show.

social.hook: Rebellion Rises came out 30 years after I saw him. I still haven't gone back.
social.caption: I genuinely love the records Ziggy Marley made after 1988 — Love Is My Religion, Rebellion Rises — and somehow that hasn't translated into a second show in 36 years.
beats: September 1988. One show. Mesa Amphitheatre. That was supposed to be the beginning.
In the years since, he released records I actually love — Rebellion Rises, Love Is My Religion.
Most artists I love, I've chased. Ziggy Marley I apparently decided to admire from a distance.
36 years of concerts, and that single 1988 night is the whole story. I don't have an explanation.

posts.headline: June 21: 35 Years Since Jimmy Buffett
posts.prose: I was at Irvine Meadows on June 21, 1991 — 35 years ago today — and I remember the sun going down over the amphitheater in a way that felt almost staged, like the sky was in on the joke. Jimmy Buffett had been playing that Southern California crowd like a warm ocean current, and somewhere between *Changes In Latitudes* and *Songs You Know By Heart*, the whole place stopped being a concert and started being a backyard party for 15,000 strangers. I didn't own a single piece of Parrothead gear, but I understood it completely by the end of the night. Some shows teach you why a fanbase exists — this was one of them.

audio.albumName: Changes In Latitudes, Changes In Attitudes

social.hook: 15,000 strangers at a backyard party I didn't know I'd been invited to
social.caption: I arrived at Irvine Meadows without a single piece of Parrothead gear. I left understanding exactly why 15,000 people had made this their religion.
beats: June 21, 1991. The sun went down over Irvine Meadows like the sky had been hired for the occasion.
Buffett moved through 'Changes In Latitudes' and 'Songs You Know By Heart' and the crowd stopped being an audience.
I owned nothing with a parrot on it. That didn't matter by the second song.
Some shows explain a fanbase from the inside. This was one of them.

posts.headline: No Doubt: Caught Once, Never Again
posts.prose: Here's something that stopped me cold when I was flipping through my oldest entries: I saw No Doubt at Disneyland in March 1988 — just two years after they formed — opening alongside The Nylons in Anaheim before virtually anyone outside Southern California knew their name. That's the only No Doubt entry in my entire archive, which means I caught them exactly once, at what had to be one of their earliest public performances, and never crossed paths with them again through *Tragic Kingdom*, *Rock Steady*, or any of the singles years. The fact that my sole sighting happened at a theme park in 1988 is the kind of detail I couldn't have invented.

social.hook: One sighting in 36 years — and it happened at a theme park.
social.caption: I saw No Doubt in March 1988, two years after they formed, opening a Disneyland bill before anyone outside Southern California knew their name. That's the only entry I have.
beats: March 1988: No Doubt were two years old and opening a Disneyland bill alongside The Nylons.
Virtually no one outside Southern California knew their name yet. I was there by accident.
Tragic Kingdom was still seven years away. Rock Steady, further still.
One entry. One night. A theme park in Anaheim. That's the whole file.

posts.headline: Garbage — Days Before Late Registration Dropped
posts.prose: In July 2005, hip-hop was about to get its most orchestral moment yet — Kanye West's Late Registration would drop just 34 days after I saw Garbage at Pacific Amphitheatre. I remember thinking how perfectly Shirley Manson's electronic-rock theatrics felt that summer, all moody synthesizers and guitar distortion. What I didn't know was that across town, Kanye was putting finishing touches on an album that would blend hip-hop with string arrangements in ways that echoed Garbage's own genre-blending DNA from the '90s. Sometimes the musical zeitgeist reveals itself in hindsight.

social.hook: 34 days before hip-hop got its most orchestral moment, Shirley Manson was already there.
social.caption: I saw Garbage at Pacific Amphitheatre on July 27, 2005 — 34 days before Late Registration dropped and Kanye proved genre-blending was everywhere that summer.
beats: July 27, 2005: moody synthesizers, guitar distortion, and Shirley Manson commanding the Pacific Amphitheatre.
34 days later, Kanye West's Late Registration would arrive — hip-hop threaded through with string arrangements.
Garbage had been bending genres since the '90s. That summer, someone across town was doing the same thing.
The musical zeitgeist doesn't announce itself. Sometimes you only see the pattern after both tickets are in a drawer.

posts.headline: Run DMC: Caught Once, Never Again
posts.prose: I caught Run DMC exactly once in my entire concert history — June 20, 1987 at Pacific Amphitheatre with the Beastie Boys opening. This was right in their Raising Hell era, when both acts were ascending rapidly, and somehow I never managed to see either of them again despite decades of concertgoing. Looking back, that single show captured lightning in a bottle: two pioneering hip-hop acts sharing a stage just as the genre was breaking into the mainstream. I can't believe I let 37 years pass without another Run DMC sighting.

social.hook: One show in 37 years — and the Beastie Boys were the opening act.
social.caption: I saw Run DMC once, June 1987, with the Beastie Boys opening. Raising Hell was still new, both acts were ascending, and somehow I never got back for a second show.
beats: June 20, 1987: Run DMC headlining, Beastie Boys opening. I did not fully appreciate what I was standing in front of.
Raising Hell had just dropped. Hip-hop was forcing its way into the mainstream, and this bill was the proof of it.
Two acts I never managed to see again — either of them — despite decades of concertgoing after that night.
37 years later, one ticket stub. Sometimes you catch lightning once and that's the whole story.

posts.headline: Sting — Days After Nevermind Dropped
posts.prose: Nevermind hit shelves on September 24th, 1991, and within days the entire rock landscape had shifted — yet there I was on October 4th, just 10 days later, watching Sting perform his polished pop-rock at Pacific Amphitheatre in Costa Mesa. I remember thinking how surreal it felt to be hearing "Fields of Gold" while the radio was still figuring out what to do with "Smells Like Teen Spirit." The timing captures this perfect moment when the old guard was still touring their greatest hits, completely unaware that the ground had already moved beneath them.

social.hook: Ten days after Nevermind dropped, the old guard had no idea the ground had already moved.
social.caption: Sting played Pacific Amphitheatre on October 4th, 1991 — ten days after Nevermind hit shelves. The radio was still figuring out what to do with 'Smells Like Teen Spirit.'
beats: Nevermind came out September 24th, 1991. Ten days later I was at a Sting show.
The radio was still mid-panic over 'Smells Like Teen Spirit' while Sting played 'Fields of Gold.'
The old guard was still touring their greatest hits, completely unaware the ground had moved.
October 4th, 1991: the last clean week before everything sounded different.

posts.headline: Siouxsie and the Banshees — Days After Achtung Baby Dropped
posts.prose: December 1991 was the month U2 shattered expectations with Achtung Baby, trading earnest anthems for industrial textures and irony — and just 33 days after that seismic shift dropped, I caught Siouxsie and the Banshees at the Universal Amphitheater. Here were two bands who'd spent the '80s proving that reinvention was survival, but Siouxsie had been mining that dark, electronic-tinged territory since 1976 while Bono was still figuring out how to be mysterious. Watching her command that stage in the shadow of U2's supposed "breakthrough" felt like a reminder of who'd been doing the real pioneering work all along.

social.hook: U2 broke the internet 33 days earlier. Siouxsie had been doing it since 1976.
social.caption: Achtung Baby dropped November 18th and everyone called it a reinvention. I saw Siouxsie at the Universal Amphitheater 33 days later, watching someone who'd been there first.
beats: Achtung Baby landed November 18, 1991 — industrial textures, irony, a supposed reinvention of rock.
Thirty-three days later I was at the Universal Amphitheater watching Siouxsie Sioux command a stage.
She'd been mining that dark, electronic territory since 1976 — while U2 were still finding their footing.
The 'breakthrough' framing felt different from the floor that night. Someone had been here the whole time.

posts.headline: April 15: 40 Years Since Blancmange
posts.prose: I saw Blancmange at Crawford Hall in Irvine 40 years ago today, and I can still picture Neil Arthur's theatrical gestures as they played through songs from Happy Families. This was during their synth-pop peak, when their blend of electronic beats and Arthur's distinctive vocals felt like the future of pop music. Crawford Hall was an intimate venue for a band that was getting significant radio play, making it feel like catching lightning in a bottle. Looking back, that April night in 1986 captured a specific moment when British new wave was reshaping American college radio.

social.hook: A synth-pop band getting radio play, in a hall that held maybe a few hundred people.
social.caption: Blancmange were all over college radio in 1986, but Crawford Hall seated a fraction of that audience. I watched Neil Arthur work through Happy Families like it was a theatre piece.
beats: April 1986: Blancmange had real radio traction, and somehow I was seeing them in a small campus hall.
Neil Arthur's stage presence was theatrical — gestures that belonged in a bigger room, delivered ten feet away.
Happy Families was the set's spine. That record still sounds like a specific moment in British synth-pop.
Crawford Hall made it feel like a secret. British new wave was rewriting American college radio, and this was the proof.

posts.headline: April 12: 40 Years Since The Alarm
posts.prose: I remember standing in that UCLA crowd 40 years ago today, watching The Alarm tear through their set with an intensity that felt almost desperate. Mike Peters had this way of leaning into the microphone like he was trying to pull every person in the venue into whatever urgent message he was delivering, and at 15, I was completely susceptible to that kind of raw conviction. They were still riding high on Strength, and you could feel the band's belief that rock music could still change the world—a notion that seemed both naive and absolutely necessary in 1986. Forty years later, I still get that same surge of adrenaline when "68 Guns" comes on shuffle.

social.hook: I was 15, and Mike Peters made me believe rock could change the world.
social.caption: Forty years ago I stood in that UCLA crowd at 15, completely undone by The Alarm's conviction. That feeling still hits every time '68 Guns' comes on shuffle.
beats: April 12, 1986: I was 15 years old and had no defenses against that kind of raw urgency.
Mike Peters leaned into the mic like he was physically pulling each person toward whatever he needed to say.
The band was still riding Strength, and the room felt the weight of their belief that rock music mattered.
The idea that music could change the world seemed naive and absolutely necessary at the same time.
Forty years on, '68 Guns' still delivers that same surge of adrenaline when it hits shuffle.

posts.headline: The Brian Setzer Orchestra: 22 Years of Shows
posts.prose: I remember discovering The Brian Setzer Orchestra at the Hard Rock Cafe in Newport Beach back in 1995, when swing revival was just starting to bubble up from the underground. That first show hooked me on Brian's rockabilly-meets-big-band sound, and I ended up catching them 4 times across 22 years, from that intimate club gig all the way to the Warner Theatre in DC in 2017. Four different venues, three different decades, but always that same electric energy when Brian strapped on his hollow-body Gretsch and the 17-piece orchestra kicked into high gear. There's something deeply satisfying about following an artist long enough to watch both of you age into the music.

social.hook: Four shows, three decades, one hollow-body Gretsch that never lost its nerve.
social.caption: I first caught the Brian Setzer Orchestra in 1995, before swing revival had a name. The last time was Washington DC in 2017 — still a 17-piece orchestra, still the same charge.
beats: Hard Rock Cafe, Newport Beach, 1995. Swing revival was underground. I had no idea I was starting a 22-year habit.
Four venues across three decades — from an intimate club gig to the Warner Theatre in DC.
Every time: Brian straps on the Gretsch, the 17-piece orchestra kicks in, and the room changes.
There's something earned about following an artist long enough to age into the music alongside him.

posts.headline: March 22: 13 Years Since Bad Religion
posts.prose: I remember walking into the 9:30 Club that March night in 2013, thirteen years ago now, and feeling like I was stepping into punk rock church. Bad Religion delivered their signature blend of melody and fury to a packed room, with Against Me!, The Bronx, and Polar Bear Club warming up the crowd beforehand. The whole evening felt like a masterclass in how punk has evolved since Bad Religion formed back in 1979, yet Greg Graffin's voice cut through the years like nothing had changed. Sometimes the best shows are the ones that remind you why you fell in love with live music in the first place.

social.hook: Greg Graffin's voice cut through 34 years like nothing had changed.
social.caption: Bad Religion formed in 1979, and by 2013 Graffin still sounded like the clock had never moved. Against Me!, The Bronx, and Polar Bear Club opened — four bands deep, one packed room.
beats: Walking into the 9:30 Club that night felt like stepping into punk rock church.
Against Me!, The Bronx, and Polar Bear Club each took the stage before the headliners arrived.
Bad Religion had been a band for 34 years by that March night — and it showed in the best way.
Greg Graffin's voice carried the same authority it always had. Some things don't erode.

posts.headline: Blancmange: Caught Once, Never Again
posts.prose: I saw Blancmange exactly once in 38 years of concertgoing — April 15, 1986 at Crawford Hall in Irvine — and somehow never crossed paths with them again. This English synth-pop duo formed in 1979 and had albums like "Happy Families" and "Mange Tout" in their catalog, yet they became the ultimate one-and-done in my concert history. It's fascinating how some artists slip through your life just once, leaving you with a single snapshot of a moment that never repeated itself.

social.hook: One show in 38 years of concertgoing — and it never happened again.
social.caption: I saw Blancmange at Crawford Hall in April 1986, when 'Happy Families' and 'Mange Tout' were both still fresh. In 38 years since, our paths never crossed a second time.
beats: April 15, 1986: Crawford Hall, Irvine. My one and only Blancmange show.
The English synth-pop duo had two albums out — 'Happy Families' and 'Mange Tout' — and felt like a band I'd see again.
38 years of concertgoing later, that night is still the only entry in the column.
Some artists pass through once and leave a single, unrepeated frame. Blancmange is mine.

posts.headline: March 23: 21 Years Since Social Distortion
posts.prose: I caught Social Distortion at the Hard Rock Hotel in Las Vegas on March 23, 2005, and I still remember how surreal it felt seeing Mike Ness's tattooed storytelling in that glitzy casino setting. Twenty-one years later, that show stands out as one of those perfect mismatches — punk rock grit against Vegas excess, like hearing "White Light White Heat White Trash" while slot machines chimed in the distance. There's something beautifully defiant about Social Distortion that made even more sense in that artificial paradise.

social.hook: Punk rock grit inside a casino, slot machines chiming in the distance.
social.caption: I saw Social Distortion at the Hard Rock Hotel in Las Vegas in 2005. Mike Ness playing 'White Light White Heat White Trash' while the slots rang — the mismatch made them sound even more defiant.
beats: March 23, 2005: Social Distortion at the Hard Rock Hotel, deep inside the Vegas casino floor.
Mike Ness's tattooed storytelling against mirrored walls and slot machine chimes — punk rock in an artificial paradise.
'White Light White Heat White Trash' in that room felt like a small, deliberate act of defiance.
Twenty-one years on, the mismatch is exactly what I remember — and why the show still holds.

posts.headline: Tears For Fears: 17 Years Between Shows
posts.prose: I remember walking out of the Universal Amphitheater in 2005 after Tears For Fears, thinking it might be the last time I'd see Roland Orzabal and Curt Smith together on stage. Seventeen years later, I found myself at the Kia Forum in Inglewood, watching them perform like no time had passed at all. The gap between those shows spans nearly two decades of my life — jobs, moves, relationships — but hearing "Mad World" again felt like stepping back into that younger version of myself. Four shows total across all these years, and somehow each one marked a different chapter of growing up with their music.

social.hook: I walked out in 2005 thinking it might be the last time.
social.caption: That 1985 show was the first of four across my life. Seventeen years passed between the third and fourth — and 'Mad World' landed exactly the same way it always had.
beats: July 1985: the first of what would become four shows across four decades of my life.
After the 2005 Universal Amphitheater show, I genuinely thought I might not see them together again.
Seventeen years later, Kia Forum in Inglewood — Roland and Curt on stage like the gap had never happened.
Each of the four shows marked a different chapter: different city, different version of me.
Hearing 'Mad World' live again felt like finding a younger version of myself still standing there.

posts.headline: Erasure — Days Before Violator Dropped
posts.prose: March 1990 was the moment synth-pop split into two futures — one heading for the dancefloor, the other for the stadium. I caught Erasure at the Forum just 8 days before Depeche Mode's Violator dropped, unknowingly witnessing the last gasps of pure pop innocence before their darker cousins conquered the world. Andy Bell's voice soared through "A Little Respect" while somewhere across town, Dave Gahan was probably rehearsing "Personal Jesus" for arenas that would dwarf this moment. Sometimes the most significant concerts are the ones that capture a scene right before it changes forever.

social.hook: 8 days before Violator dropped, I was watching the other future.
social.caption: Erasure played 'A Little Respect' on March 11, 1990. Depeche Mode's Violator arrived eight days later and changed which direction synth-pop went.
beats: March 1990: synth-pop was about to split into two very different futures.
I was at the Forum for Erasure — pure pop, Andy Bell's voice at full altitude.
Eight days later, Violator arrived and Depeche Mode claimed the stadiums.
I didn't know it at the time. That's what makes the ticket stub matter.

posts.headline: The Alarm: Caught Once, Never Again
posts.prose: I caught The Alarm exactly once in my entire concert-going life — April 12, 1986 at UCLA — and somehow never circled back to them again across nearly four decades of shows. This Welsh alternative rock band, formed in 1981, was riding high on their Strength album when I saw them, yet they became a complete one-and-done in my archive despite releasing Eye of the Hurricane the following year. It's genuinely puzzling how a band can make enough of an impression to get me to a show, then vanish entirely from my radar for the next 38 years.

social.hook: One show in 38 years of concert-going, and I still can't explain why.
social.caption: The Alarm were touring behind Strength when I caught them at UCLA in April 1986. They released Eye of the Hurricane the following year, and I never saw them again.
beats: April 1986: The Alarm were touring behind Strength, and I bought a ticket.
That night at UCLA is the only entry they have in nearly four decades of my archive.
Eye of the Hurricane came out the following year. I didn't go back.
Some bands you see once, file away, and never quite return to. The Alarm is my clearest example.

posts.headline: Echo and the Bunnymen: 26 Years Between Shows
posts.prose: I caught Echo and the Bunnymen at Irvine Meadows in 1984, when their post-punk atmospherics still felt urgent and new. Twenty-six years passed before I saw them again — a quarter-century gap that took me from California amphitheaters to a cramped club in D.C. called The Black Cat in 2010. By then, Ian McCulloch's voice had weathered but the songs from *Porcupine* and those early albums still carried that same moody weight. Sometimes the longest waits between shows make you appreciate how certain bands become part of your internal soundtrack, whether you're actively listening or not.

social.hook: A quarter-century gap, then a cramped D.C. club instead of a California amphitheater.
social.caption: I saw Echo and the Bunnymen at Irvine Meadows in 1984, then not again until The Black Cat in Washington D.C. in 2010 — 26 years and a very different room.
beats: Irvine Meadows, 1984: post-punk atmospherics that still felt urgent and genuinely new.
Then nothing for 26 years — a quarter-century of those songs living only in my head.
The return was The Black Cat in D.C., 2010: a cramped club, a world away from a California amphitheater.
Ian McCulloch's voice had weathered, but the songs from Porcupine still carried the same moody weight.

posts.headline: No Doubt — Days Before It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back Dropped
posts.prose: Hip-hop was about to get its political manifesto, but I was watching a ska band from Orange County play at the happiest place on earth. I caught No Doubt at Disneyland on March 4, 1988, just 37 days before Public Enemy would drop It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back and change everything about what rap could say and do. While Chuck D was putting the finishing touches on hip-hop's first true political landmark, I was experiencing the early stirrings of what would become the ska revival, watching Gwen Stefani and company work through their sound in front of families with mouse ears. Two completely different revolutions brewing at the same time — one I witnessed firsthand, the other I'd discover when it hit like a manifesto five weeks later.

social.hook: 37 days before hip-hop's political manifesto dropped, I was watching ska at Disneyland.
social.caption: No Doubt played Disneyland on March 4, 1988, 37 days before Public Enemy released It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back. Two revolutions, same five weeks.
beats: March 4, 1988: No Doubt playing Disneyland, families in mouse ears watching a ska band find its sound.
Thirty-seven days away, Chuck D was finishing hip-hop's first true political landmark.
Public Enemy's It Takes a Nation of Millions dropped April 10, 1988 — and changed what rap could say.
I witnessed one revolution live. The other hit like a manifesto five weeks later.
Two completely different upheavals, brewing in the same narrow window of five weeks.

posts.headline: Bruce Springsteen: Caught Once, Never Again
posts.prose: I saw Bruce Springsteen exactly once in my entire concert-going life — September 29, 1985 at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum during the Born in the U.S.A. tour. Despite attending hundreds of shows across four decades, The Boss never crossed my path again, making him one of the most glaring single-sighting artists in my archive. It's almost impossible to believe that someone who built a career on marathon three-hour shows and relentless touring somehow became my ultimate one-and-done experience. Sometimes the biggest names leave the smallest footprints.

social.hook: Hundreds of shows across four decades. He played three-hour sets. We never crossed paths again.
social.caption: I saw Bruce Springsteen once — Born in the U.S.A. tour, 1985 — and in hundreds of shows since, he never crossed my path again. One ticket stub in forty years.
beats: September 29, 1985: the Born in the U.S.A. tour at its peak, one of the biggest acts in the world.
He was already famous for marathon sets — three hours, no intermission, no concessions made.
I kept going to shows. Hundreds of them, across four decades. He never came up again.
One ticket stub. That's the whole Springsteen section of my archive.

posts.headline: UB40: 35 Years Between Shows
posts.prose: I saw UB40 at Pacific Amphitheatre in 1988, back when "Red Red Wine" was still fresh and their reggae-pop was everywhere on the radio. Thirty-five years passed before I caught them again at the Peacock Theater in 2023 — the longest gap between any artist in my concert history. Walking into that LA venue, I wondered if they'd still have that Birmingham-meets-Jamaica energy that made their Labour of Love covers so infectious. Time had changed us both, but the music hit exactly the same way it did in Costa Mesa all those decades ago.

social.hook: 35 years between ticket stubs — the longest gap in my entire concert history.
social.caption: I saw UB40 at Pacific Amphitheatre in 1988, when 'Red Red Wine' was still on the radio. Peacock Theater in 2023, and it landed exactly the same way.
beats: Pacific Amphitheatre, 1988. 'Red Red Wine' was everywhere, and UB40's reggae-pop felt like it owned the summer.
Then nothing — thirty-five years, the longest stretch between any artist I've ever seen twice.
Walking into Peacock Theater in 2023, I wasn't sure the Birmingham-meets-Jamaica energy would survive the gap.
It did. The Labour of Love covers hit exactly the same way they had in Costa Mesa all those decades before.

posts.headline: The Brian Setzer Orchestra: A Jazz/Blues Outlier in a Rock / Electronic / Reggae Archive
posts.prose: I just discovered that The Brian Setzer Orchestra represents my only swing and blues shows in an archive that's 86% rock, electronic, and reggae. Three shows across 22 years — Hard Rock Cafe in Newport Beach in 1995, Universal Amphitheater in 2002, and the Warner Theatre in DC in 2017 — stand as complete genre outliers in my concert history. It's fascinating that my musical wandering led me to catch them during three different decades, from the "Dirty Boogie" era through their Christmas tours. Sometimes the most revealing thing about your taste is what doesn't fit the pattern.

social.hook: Three decades of swing in an archive that's 86% rock, electronic, and reggae.
social.caption: The Brian Setzer Orchestra is my only swing and blues act across 40 years of shows. Three nights, three decades — Newport Beach, Los Angeles, DC — all genre outliers.
beats: My archive runs 86% rock, electronic, and reggae. BSO is the lone swing and blues entry.
Newport Beach in 1995 was the 'Dirty Boogie' era — before the Christmas tours made them a seasonal institution.
Universal Amphitheater in 2002, then Warner Theatre in DC in 2017. Three decades, one thread.
Sometimes what doesn't fit the pattern tells you more about your taste than everything that does.

posts.headline: The Brian Setzer Orchestra — Days After The Bends Dropped
posts.prose: March 1995 was a pivotal moment in rock history — Radiohead had just released The Bends, the album that signaled they were doing something different from everyone else, and I found myself at the Hard Rock Cafe in Newport Beach just 13 days later watching The Brian Setzer Orchestra swing through their rockabilly revival. While Thom Yorke was pushing guitar music into uncharted emotional territory, I was experiencing the opposite impulse: Brian Setzer's calculated nostalgia, all pompadour and upright bass, pulling rock back to its 1950s roots. The timing feels like a perfect snapshot of mid-'90s music culture — innovation and retro-fetishism existing in the same two-week span, both trying to solve the problem of what rock could be after grunge.

social.hook: Radiohead released The Bends 13 days before this show. Both were solving the same problem.
social.caption: The Bends landed on March 13, 1995. Thirteen days later I was watching Brian Setzer pull rock in the opposite direction — pompadour, upright bass, pure 1950s revival.
beats: March 13, 1995: Radiohead releases The Bends and points guitar music somewhere new.
Thirteen days later I'm at the Hard Rock Cafe in Newport Beach watching Brian Setzer do the opposite.
Pompadour, upright bass, rockabilly swing — a deliberate argument for where rock began.
Two answers to the same post-grunge question, two weeks apart. Neither one wrong.

posts.headline: Social Distortion + 14 More: 2018 Festival Bill
posts.prose: California punk's founding fathers assembled for what felt like a family reunion at Huntington State Beach in 2018, with Social Distortion, Bad Religion, and 13 other acts spanning four decades of West Coast rebellion. I witnessed bands that had been shaping punk since 1979 sharing the same sand with newer torchbearers like The Interrupters, creating this perfect cross-generational snapshot of the scene's evolution. Seeing Fear and Suicidal Tendencies on the same bill as Black Rebel Motorcycle Club reminded me how punk's DNA keeps mutating while staying fundamentally defiant. Standing on that beach with 15 bands cycling through, I felt like I was getting a master class in how Southern California invented its own brand of sunny nihilism.

social.hook: 15 bands, one beach, forty years of West Coast punk on a single Sunday.
social.caption: Fourteen acts on one bill at Huntington State Beach put 1979-era originators on the same sand as bands still writing their first chapters. The note is up — it holds the full reckoning.
beats: October 2018: fifteen bands cycled through Huntington State Beach in a single afternoon.
Social Distortion and Bad Religion carried 1979 on their backs. The Interrupters carried whatever comes next.
Fear and Suicidal Tendencies on the same bill as Black Rebel Motorcycle Club — punk's DNA, visibly mutating.
Four decades of West Coast rebellion compressed into one stretch of sand. The archive has the full account.

posts.headline: Depeche Mode: 18 Years Between Shows
posts.prose: I remember walking out of Staples Center in November 2005 after seeing Depeche Mode, never imagining it would be 18 years before I'd see them again. Life happened — moves, kids, priorities shifted — and suddenly it was 2023 and I was driving to the Kia Forum in Inglewood, practically the same neighborhood where I'd last seen them. The gap felt surreal, like I was reconnecting with a version of myself I'd almost forgotten. Eighteen years is long enough to raise a child, but Dave Gahan's voice still hit exactly the same way it did when I was younger.

social.hook: 18 years apart, practically the same neighborhood, exactly the same voice.
social.caption: I saw Depeche Mode at Staples Center in November 2005, then drove to the Kia Forum in Inglewood in 2023 — nearly the same corner of LA, nearly two decades later. Dave Gahan's voice didn't move.
beats: Walking out of Staples Center in 2005, I had no idea I'd just started an 18-year wait.
Life filled the gap — moves, kids, priorities — and then it was 2023 and I was back in Inglewood.
The Kia Forum sits in practically the same neighborhood as Staples Center. The geography barely changed.
Eighteen years is long enough to raise a child. Dave Gahan's voice landed exactly the same way it always had.

posts.headline: Universal Amphitheater: 5 Shows Before It Was Demolished
posts.prose: Five shows at the Universal Amphitheater across 16 years, and I had no idea I was watching a clock run down. I opened my history there with Howard Jones in July 1989 and closed it with Tears For Fears in November 2005 — and then the place was gone, demolished after that last night. Four different artists, one venue that quietly threaded through a big slice of my concert life, and I never once thought of it as a place I should be paying closer attention to. Turns out Tears For Fears gave me the farewell show I didn't know I needed.

social.hook: Universal Amphitheater was demolished. My last night there was Tears For Fears in 2005.
social.caption: I opened my history at Universal Amphitheater with Howard Jones in 1989 and closed it with Tears For Fears in 2005 — the farewell show I didn't know I was having.
beats: Five shows at Universal Amphitheater across 16 years, four different artists, zero awareness I was running out of time.
It started with Howard Jones in July 1989. I was just going to a show. I had no idea the room would matter.
Siouxsie and the Banshees. The Brian Setzer Orchestra. Each one felt like its own night, not part of a pattern.
Tears For Fears in November 2005 turned out to be the last. The venue was demolished after that.
I never thought of Universal Amphitheater as a place I should pay closer attention to. Turns out I should have.

posts.headline: The Cure + 14 More: 2003 Festival Bill
posts.prose: This 2003 festival captured new wave's full evolution — from The Cure's goth-pop mastery to Duran Duran's synth glamour, with Dashboard Confessional and Interpol representing where alternative rock was heading next. I witnessed 15 acts spanning three decades of post-punk DNA, from the original wave (Echo and the Bunnymen, Psychedelic Furs) through the '90s survivors (Violent Femmes) to the emerging indie darlings (Kings of Leon, Hot Hot Heat). The Hyundai Pavilion became a living museum of how Robert Smith's melancholy had spawned an entire musical ecosystem. Standing there in San Bernardino, I realized I wasn't just watching a festival — I was seeing the alternative rock family tree in full bloom.

social.hook: 15 acts, three decades of post-punk DNA, one afternoon in the Inland Empire.
social.caption: Fifteen acts shared one stage in San Bernardino, from Echo & the Bunnymen to Kings of Leon. The whole alternative family tree, in bloom on a single afternoon.
beats: September 20, 2003: 15 acts on one bill, spanning new wave's first wave through its newest heirs.
The Cure anchored the night, but Interpol and Kings of Leon were the argument about what came next.
Duran Duran's synth glamour, the Psychedelic Furs' jangle, Dashboard Confessional's ache — all on the same card.
Hyundai Pavilion held the original wave and the inheritors at once. The distance between them was smaller than expected.
I left San Bernardino understanding Robert Smith's melancholy as a root system, not just a sound.

posts.headline: Howard Jones: 17 Years Between Shows
posts.prose: I remember standing in the Universal Amphitheater in 1989, watching Howard Jones perform what I didn't know would be his last show in my collection for nearly two decades. When I finally saw him again in 2006 at the intimate Coach House in San Juan Capistrano, it felt like reconnecting with an old friend after years of silence. That 17-year gap represents the longest drought between any artist's appearances in my concert history. The shift from arena to club venue somehow made his synth-pop anthems feel more personal, like he was playing just for the handful of us who had waited all those years.

social.hook: Seventeen years later, he was playing twenty feet away.
social.caption: I saw Howard Jones at Universal Amphitheater in 1989 and didn't catch him again until 2006 — The Coach House in San Juan Capistrano, maybe 200 people in the room.
beats: Universal Amphitheater, 1989. Arena lights, a proper crowd, synth-pop filling every seat.
Then nothing. Seventeen years of nothing — the longest gap between any artist in my entire archive.
The Coach House, San Juan Capistrano, 2006. Intimate enough to see his hands on the keys.
Same songs. Completely different scale. They landed harder in the small room than they ever did in the arena.

posts.headline: Irvine Meadows: 16 Shows Before It Was Demolished
posts.prose: I discovered I saw 16 shows at Irvine Meadows between 1984 and 2003, from Adam Ant's April '84 performance to Peter Gabriel in June 2003, before the venue was demolished in 2016. What strikes me is how this amphitheater captured a specific era — my concert history there reads like a New Wave and post-punk time capsule, heavy on acts like Thompson Twins, Billy Idol, Echo and the Bunnymen, and Depeche Mode. Thirteen different artists across nearly two decades, and now it's all tract housing where those summer nights used to echo with synthesizers and guitar feedback.

social.hook: Irvine Meadows held 16 of my shows — then became tract housing in 2016.
social.caption: Thirteen artists, nearly two decades, one amphitheater: Adam Ant in April '84 to Peter Gabriel in June 2003. Irvine Meadows is gone, but my stubs are a New Wave time capsule.
beats: Adam Ant opened my Irvine Meadows account in April 1984. I had no idea I'd be back 15 more times.
Thompson Twins, Billy Idol, Echo & The Bunnymen, Depeche Mode — the setlist of a synthesizer summer.
16 shows, 13 artists, 19 years. The place shaped a whole chapter of how I heard music.
Peter Gabriel closed it out for me in June 2003. The venue itself lasted until 2016.
Now it's tract housing. Irvine Meadows held those summer nights — and my records are what's left.

posts.headline: Peter Gabriel + 11 More: 1993 Festival Bill
posts.prose: The early '90s were the golden age of world music crossover, when MTV and major festivals finally opened their doors to artists like Ziggy Marley, The Drummers of Burundi, and Sinéad O'Connor sharing the same bill. I caught this spectacular 12-artist lineup at the Olympic Velodrome in Carson in September 1993, headlined by Peter Gabriel during his peak "So" era. The sheer diversity was staggering — from Crowded House's jangly pop-rock to Jah Wobble's experimental dub, from P.M. Dawn's hip-hop soul to the traditional rhythms of Burundi. Looking back, it feels like witnessing a brief moment when the music industry genuinely believed in bringing the world together on one stage.

social.hook: Twelve artists, one stage, the brief window when world music crossed over.
social.caption: I was at the Olympic Velodrome in September 1993 for a 12-artist bill that put The Drummers of Burundi and P.M. Dawn on the same afternoon. It felt like the industry meaning it.
beats: September 1993: twelve artists, one stage in Carson — a lineup that shouldn't have worked and completely did.
Peter Gabriel headlined, deep into the 'So' era. Sinéad O'Connor and Ziggy Marley were on the same bill.
P.M. Dawn. Jah Wobble. The Drummers of Burundi. Crowded House. All in one afternoon.
It was a brief window when major festivals genuinely tried to bring the world together. I was there for it.

posts.headline: New Order: 37 Years Between Shows
posts.prose: I saw New Order at Irvine Meadows in 1985 when I was just getting into their sound — that perfect blend of post-punk edge and dance floor pulse that made Brotherhood feel so essential. Then nothing. Thirty-seven years passed before I caught them again at the Hollywood Bowl in 2022, and walking into that venue, I couldn't help but think about how much had changed in both our lives since that summer night in Orange County. The music hit just as hard, but I was definitely standing in a very different place to receive it.

social.hook: Thirty-seven years is a long time to carry a first impression.
social.caption: I first saw New Order at Irvine Meadows in 1985 and didn't catch them again until the Hollywood Bowl in 2022. The music held; I was the one who had changed.
beats: August 1985: I was just finding my footing with New Order, drawn in by that post-punk edge meeting the dance floor.
Irvine Meadows that summer was the whole introduction — the first time that sound landed on me in person.
Then thirty-seven years went by before I stood in front of them again, this time at the Hollywood Bowl.
Same band. The music hit just as hard. I was standing in a very different place to receive it.

posts.headline: Billy Idol: Caught Once, Never Again
posts.prose: I saw Billy Idol exactly once in four decades of concertgoing — August 13, 1984 at Irvine Meadows — and somehow never crossed paths with him again. This strikes me as nearly impossible given how ubiquitous he became after *Rebel Yell*, yet my archive shows a complete Billy Idol drought from 1985 to present. Maybe I was unconsciously avoiding the crowds, or maybe our touring schedules just never aligned, but it's wild that a single summer night in Orange County represents my entire Billy Idol experience.

social.hook: One show in forty years — and it was three months after Rebel Yell dropped.
social.caption: I saw Billy Idol at Irvine Meadows in August 1984 and never caught him again. Rebel Yell had been out since November 1983, and he was everywhere after that — just never where I was.
beats: August 1984: Rebel Yell was nine months old and Billy Idol was becoming inescapable.
One night at Irvine Meadows and then nothing — not once in the four decades since.
That's a complete drought across the peak of his career, the MTV years, every tour.
One summer night in Orange County is the whole of my Billy Idol archive.

posts.headline: Thompson Twins in 1984: The Year of 1984 Los Angeles Summer Olympics
posts.prose: Los Angeles in 1984 was electric with Olympic fever, and the new wave acts flooding Irvine Meadows that year captured that same restless energy. I saw Thompson Twins in May, right in the thick of it — part of a four-show run at the venue that also brought Adam Ant, Billy Idol, and Echo and the Bunnymen between April and September. The Thompson Twins were riding high on "Into the Gap," their synth-pop perfectly matching the city's futuristic Olympic optimism. Looking back, those 4 concerts feel like a snapshot of new wave's peak moment, when MTV and the Games made everything feel possible.

social.hook: Four new wave shows, one Olympic summer, one outdoor amphitheater.
social.caption: Irvine Meadows ran four new wave nights between April and September 1984. Thompson Twins, Adam Ant, Billy Idol, Echo and the Bunnymen — all of it against an Olympic summer.
beats: Los Angeles in 1984 was mid-sprint toward the Summer Olympics, and the city felt it everywhere.
Irvine Meadows hosted four new wave shows that year: Thompson Twins, Adam Ant, Billy Idol, Echo and the Bunnymen.
The Thompson Twins came through in May, riding 'Into the Gap' into a crowd already primed for something electric.
MTV and the Olympics made 1984 feel like a hinge point. Those four nights are the proof I was there for it.

posts.headline: Duran Duran: 21 Years Between Shows
posts.prose: I remember standing at Irvine Meadows in 1987 watching Duran Duran, not knowing it would be 21 years before I'd see them again. That Nokia Center show in 2008 felt like stepping into a time machine — Simon Le Bon's voice cutting through two decades of silence, bringing back memories of new wave summers and MTV afternoons. Three shows total across my concert history, but that middle gap speaks volumes about how life can drift you away from the bands that once defined your weekends. Sometimes the longest waits make for the sweetest reunions.

social.hook: Simon Le Bon's voice crossed 21 years like they hadn't passed at all.
social.caption: I first saw Duran Duran at Irvine Meadows in 1987, when new wave was still the air we breathed. The Nokia Center in 2008 was the reunion — and his voice made the gap disappear.
beats: Irvine Meadows, July 1987. New wave was at its peak and Duran Duran owned the summer.
Then life moved. Twenty-one years of it, without a single show between.
Nokia Center, 2008. Simon Le Bon opened his mouth and the two decades folded flat.
Three shows across my whole history with this band — and that middle silence is the loudest part of the story.

posts.headline: Stryper: Caught Once, Never Again
posts.prose: I saw Stryper exactly once in my entire concert-going life — May 17, 1985 at Knots Berry Farm in Buena Park. This was just two years after they formed, before "To Hell with the Devil" would make them the most successful Christian metal band of the era. Something about that single sighting feels perfectly calibrated: I caught them at exactly the right moment, then never felt compelled to return. Maybe once was enough to appreciate the novelty of headbanging to hymns in an amusement park.

social.hook: Two years in, before the album that changed everything — and I never went back.
social.caption: I saw them in 1985, two years after they formed and still a year before 'To Hell with the Devil.' One show in an amusement park was exactly enough.
beats: May 17, 1985: Stryper at an amusement park in Buena Park, two years after they formed.
'To Hell with the Devil' was still a year away — this was before the breakthrough.
Headbanging to hymns on a theme park stage is a specific experience I can't quite explain.
One show. Never went back. Somehow that feels like exactly the right call.

posts.headline: The Human League + 8 More: 2018 Festival Bill
posts.prose: The 2018 nostalgia festival circuit became a time machine for those of us who lived through the new wave explosion of the early '80s. I caught this 9-band bill at Huntington State Beach, headlined by The Human League with 8 supporting acts including The Alarm, Dramarama, and Naked Eyes — essentially a greatest hits compilation of synth-pop and alternative rock from 1977 to 1987. What struck me wasn't just the concentrated dose of my teenage soundtrack, but how these songs that once felt so futuristic now carried the warm patina of shared memory. Standing on that beach, surrounded by fellow Gen-Xers singing along to "Don't You (Forget About Me)" vibes, I realized we'd become our parents at the oldies show.

social.hook: Nine bands. One beach. The decade that refused to end.
social.caption: Nine acts across a single afternoon at Huntington State Beach made 1977–1987 feel like last summer. Somewhere between The Alarm and The Human League, I became my parents at the oldies show.
beats: Nine bands on one bill: The Human League headlining, The Alarm, Dramarama, Naked Eyes, and five more.
The set list covered a full decade — 1977 to 1987 — without a gap in the room's memory.
Songs that once sounded like the future now carried the warm weight of shared nostalgia.
Standing on that beach, surrounded by fellow Gen-Xers singing every word, the irony landed hard.
We'd become exactly what we once rolled our eyes at: our parents at the oldies show.

posts.headline: The Smithereens: 21 Years Between Shows
posts.prose: I saw The Smithereens at The Celebrity Theatre in Anaheim in 1992, then didn't catch them again until 21 years later at The Hamilton Live in Washington. That's a gap that spans my entire twenties and thirties — I was a different person entirely by the time I heard those power-pop hooks again. It's strange how some bands just vanish from your radar, even when they keep making music. Sometimes the longest breaks make the reunion feel like discovering an old friend's phone number in a jacket pocket.

social.hook: 21 years — my entire twenties and thirties — between two shows.
social.caption: I saw The Smithereens in Anaheim in 1992, then not again until Washington in 2013. Two decades of their records playing without me in a room watching them make it.
beats: Celebrity Theatre, Anaheim, June 1992. Power-pop hooks loud enough to rearrange something in my chest.
Then nothing. Not because they stopped — they kept making music. I just lost the thread somewhere in my twenties.
21 years later: The Hamilton Live in Washington. A different city, a different version of me.
Some reunions feel like finding an old friend's number in a jacket you hadn't worn in a decade. This was that.

posts.headline: Wham!: Caught Once, Never Again
posts.prose: I saw Wham! exactly once in my entire concert-going history — August 30, 1985 at Hollywood Park Racetrack in Inglewood — and somehow never crossed paths with them again despite decades of shows. This was right in their "Make It Big" era, with Chaka Khan and Katrina and the Waves opening, yet they became the ultimate one-and-done in my archive. social.caption: One show, August 1985, and that was it — Wham! played Hollywood Park Racetrack during the Make It Big era and somehow never appeared in my concert life again across decades of shows.
beats: August 30, 1985: Hollywood Park Racetrack, Inglewood. Chaka Khan and Katrina and the Waves opened the night.
This was the Make It Big era — Wham! at full commercial height, one of the biggest pop acts on the planet.
I was there for all of it. And then, across every show I attended after that, they simply never came back around.
One entry in forty years of records. The most massive one-and-done in my entire archive.

posts.headline: Foo Fighters + 9 More: 2015 Festival Bill
posts.prose: The 4th of July 2015 at RFK Stadium was one of those rare festival bills that read like a cross-section of American music itself — blues legend Buddy Guy sharing the stage with Foo Fighters, Heart bridging classic and alternative rock, LL Cool J representing hip-hop's golden age, all anchored by the go-go sounds of Trouble Funk. I caught this 10-artist extravaganza during Foo Fighters' peak touring years, just as they were cementing their status as arena headliners more than two decades after Dave Grohl formed the band in 1994. The sheer breadth of genres — from Buddy Guy's six decades of blues mastery to DJ Z-Trip's turntable wizardry — felt like watching the soundtrack to America unfold in real time on Independence Day.

social.hook: Ten acts, six decades of blues, and a go-go band that never left D.C.
social.caption: Trouble Funk anchored the local end of a bill that also ran from Buddy Guy's blues to LL Cool J's hip-hop. I saw all ten acts at RFK on the Fourth of July.

Buddy Guy brought six decades of blues. Trouble Funk brought the sound that belongs to that city.
Heart and Joan Jett held the rock middle. LL Cool J represented hip-hop's golden age. DJ Z-Trip held it all together.
Foo Fighters were deep into their arena-headliner years by then — more than two decades after Grohl formed the band.
Independence Day, Washington D.C., the whole American soundtrack playing live. Some bills just make sense.

posts.headline: Depeche Mode: 38 Years of Shows
posts.prose: I still remember walking into Irvine Meadows in 1985 for my first Depeche Mode show, not knowing I was starting something that would span 38 years and four decades of my concert-going life. Five shows across California venues, from that early synthpop energy through their Violator era and beyond, each one marking a different chapter of both their evolution and mine. social.hook: Five shows. Thirty-eight years. Still counting.
social.caption: I walked into Irvine Meadows in 1985 not knowing I was starting a 38-year run. The most recent was last year at the Kia Forum in Inglewood — five shows, four decades.
beats: March 31, 1985: my first Depeche Mode show, Irvine Meadows. I was 18 and had no idea what I was starting.
Five shows across California venues — each one a different chapter of their evolution and mine.
The Violator era landed somewhere in the middle, and the band that showed up was not the same band I'd first seen.
Last year at the Kia Forum in Inglewood, I kept thinking about that 18-year-old at Irvine Meadows.
Some artists you see once. Others become a parallel soundtrack to your entire adult life. This is the latter.

posts.headline: The Smithereens in 1992: The Year of Los Angeles uprising after the Rodney King verdict
posts.prose: The Smithereens were hitting their stride in 1992, riding the wave of their most successful period, when I caught them at The Celebrity Theatre in Anaheim that June. The streets that summer were fractured and raw after the acquittal, and going out felt charged with something unresolved. I remember the drive down to Orange County feeling different somehow — like the whole region was still processing what had happened just weeks before. The Smithereens' blend of power pop and heartland rock felt like the right soundtrack for that moment, their earnest melodies cutting through the tension that lingered in the California air.

social.hook: Orange County, six weeks after the verdict — going out felt charged
social.caption: The Smithereens at Celebrity Theatre, June 4, 1992. The acquittal was still weeks old, and the drive down from LA felt like the whole region was mid-sentence.
beats: April 29, 1992: the acquittal. By June 4, the city was still mid-sentence.
The drive to Anaheim that night felt different — Orange County, but the same unsettled air.
Power pop and heartland rock turned out to be the right soundtrack for unresolved things.
The Smithereens were at their commercial peak that year. The room knew it.

posts.headline: Howard Jones: 39 Years of Shows
posts.prose: I first caught Howard Jones at Irvine Meadows in 1985, right in the thick of his "Dream Into Action" era when those synthesizer hooks were everywhere. What strikes me now is how I kept coming back — six shows across 39 years, from that outdoor amphitheater in Orange County to the YouTube Theatre in Inglewood just this past August. There's something about his earnest optimism and those unmistakable keyboard melodies that pulls me back decade after decade. I suppose some artists just become part of your personal soundtrack, whether you plan it or not.

social.hook: Six shows. Thirty-nine years. Still the same keyboard melodies pulling me back.
social.caption: I first saw Howard Jones in 1985 and returned five more times over 39 years. Some artists just become part of your personal soundtrack whether you plan it or not.
beats: June 1985: Howard Jones at Irvine Meadows, deep in the Dream Into Action era, synth hooks everywhere.
I didn't plan a 39-year relationship with his catalog. I just kept buying tickets.
Six shows, multiple decades, Orange County to Inglewood — the same earnest optimism each time.
Some artists earn a place in your personal soundtrack and simply never leave it.

posts.headline: Maxi Priest + 6 More: 1991 Festival Bill
posts.prose: This was reggae's moment in American mainstream consciousness, and I caught a perfect snapshot of it at Pacific Amphitheatre in June 1991. Maxi Priest was riding high with crossover hits, headlining over a seven-artist bill that included Dennis Brown and Andrew Tosh — Peter Tosh's son, carrying forward his father's legacy. I remember the crowd being surprisingly diverse for Orange County, drawn by reggae's growing radio presence around that time. What struck me most was how the music unified this massive outdoor crowd, from the opening act through Priest's closing set under the California stars.

social.hook: Seven artists, one night, and reggae briefly owned Orange County
social.caption: Dennis Brown and Peter Tosh's son Andrew were on the same bill — a snapshot of the moment reggae was cracking American radio. Pacific Amphitheatre held the whole thing together.
beats: June 1991: reggae was crossing over, and this seven-artist bill caught that moment at its peak.
Andrew Tosh was on that stage — Peter's son, carrying the name and the weight of it.
Dennis Brown sharing a bill with Maxi Priest felt like the roots and the crossover in the same breath.
The crowd at Pacific Amphitheatre was more diverse than Orange County usually delivered. The music did that.
Priest closed it under open California sky. Seven acts, one through-line, and I was there for all of it.

posts.headline: Social Distortion: 34 Years of Shows
posts.prose: I first caught Social Distortion at Cal State Fullerton in 1990, back when Mike Ness was still carving out that distinctive sound that would define them through White Light White Heat White Trash and beyond. Eight shows across 34 years might not sound like devotion, but with Social D, each one felt like checking in with an old friend who'd weathered the same storms. My most recent show was just this past December at The Belasco, and hearing those same punk rock anthems that shaped my college years still hit with the same raw honesty. There's something comforting about a band that refuses to reinvent itself—they just keep getting better at being exactly who they've always been.

social.hook: Eight shows and Mike Ness never once pretended to be anyone else.
social.caption: I started at Cal State Fullerton in 1990 and closed the loop at The Belasco in December 2024. Same punk rock honesty, 34 years apart.
beats: Cal State Fullerton, 1990. Mike Ness was still shaping the sound that would carry Social D for decades.
Eight shows across 34 years isn't a streak — it's more like checking in when you need to be reminded.
White Light White Heat White Trash landed somewhere between those early shows and the ones that followed.
The Belasco, December 2024. The anthems from my college years hit exactly as hard as I needed them to.
Some bands chase reinvention. Social D just kept getting better at being exactly who they always were.

posts.headline: Oingo Boingo + 5 More: 1987 Festival Bill
posts.prose: This was the era when alternative rock was still finding its footing alongside new wave's final flourishes — and somehow I caught all of it on one stage in Tijuana. Six acts that would define different corners of the late-80s landscape: Oingo Boingo riding high on "Dead Man's Party," The Bangles at their commercial peak, Squeeze's sophisticated pop craft, and Australia's Hoodoo Gurus bringing their garage rock energy just five years after forming. I remember the surreal border-crossing pilgrimage to Caliente Racetrack, where Chris Isaak's crooning and The Fixx's synth-rock completed this unlikely but perfect snapshot of 1987's musical diversity. Looking back, it feels like witnessing a changing of the guard I didn't even know was happening.

social.hook: Six bands, one racetrack, one border crossing I'll never forget
social.caption: Six acts on one stage at a racetrack in Tijuana — Oingo Boingo, The Bangles, Squeeze, and three more. A single afternoon that felt like a survey of everything alternative rock was becoming.
beats: June 30, 1987: crossing the border to catch six bands at a horse racing venue felt absurd. It wasn't.
Oingo Boingo, The Bangles, and Squeeze alone would have been enough. Then add Chris Isaak, The Fixx, and Hoodoo Gurus.
Hoodoo Gurus had only formed five years earlier. Somehow they belonged on that stage as much as anyone.
Chris Isaak's croon next to The Fixx's synths next to garage rock — the bill shouldn't have worked. It did.
I didn't know I was watching a changing of the guard. That's usually how those moments go.

posts.headline: Crowded House: From Opener to Headliner
posts.prose: Crowded House's trajectory from Melbourne alt-rock darlings to enduring pop craftsmen spans exactly the 30 years between when I saw them open for Peter Gabriel at the Olympic Velodrome in 1993 and headline The Wiltern in 2023. That first show came around the time *Woodface* had established them as more than just Neil Finn's post-Split Enz project, but they were still very much the supporting act in a massive arena. Three decades later, watching them command their own stage at the Wiltern felt like witnessing the full arc of a band that never chased trends but simply outlasted them. Some artists earn their headliner status through persistence and craft rather than flash.

social.hook: Opener in 1993, headliner in 2023 — thirty years, no shortcuts.
social.caption: I first saw Crowded House supporting Peter Gabriel at the Olympic Velodrome, when Woodface was still fresh. Thirty years later they headlined the Wiltern, and every minute of it felt earned.
beats: September 1993: Crowded House were the support act for Peter Gabriel at the Olympic Velodrome in Carson.
Woodface had given them a foothold, but the night still belonged to Gabriel — they were there to warm up his crowd.
Thirty years later, the Wiltern was entirely theirs. Same band, same craft, no reinvention required.
Some acts chase the moment. Crowded House just kept making the music until the moment caught up with them.

posts.headline: My West Coast Chapter: 26 Concerts Over 11 Years
posts.prose: I still remember standing at Irvine Meadows in October 1988, watching Oingo Boingo tear through the night air, thinking I had no idea what the next 11 years of California shows would look like. That first West Coast concert cracked something open — 26 shows across 16 venues, from Irvine to Redondo Beach, two full decades bleeding into each other. I caught 22 different artists during that chapter, ending quietly at Club Caprice in 1999 with Alien Fashion Show, which is honestly a perfect last entry for a run that started with Oingo Boingo. Some chapters close before you realize they've closed.

social.hook: 26 shows, 16 venues, 22 artists — and I didn't know it had started yet.
social.caption: I was standing at Irvine Meadows in October 1988 with no idea I'd just opened an 11-year California chapter. It closed in 1999 at Club Caprice with Alien Fashion Show.
beats: Oingo Boingo at Irvine Meadows, October 1988 — I had no idea I was starting something.
Over 11 years, 26 West Coast shows took me across 16 venues from Irvine to Redondo Beach.
22 different artists filled that chapter: Depeche Mode, Peter Gabriel, Sting, Erasure, and more.
It ended quietly in 1999 — Club Caprice, Alien Fashion Show, no fanfare.
Some chapters close before you realize they've closed. This one finally has a cover.

posts.headline: Squeeze: From Opener to Headliner
posts.prose: Few bands embodied the scrappy spirit of new wave quite like Squeeze, and my concert history accidentally documented their long climb from opening act to headliner. I first saw them opening for Oingo Boingo at a racetrack in Tijuana in 1987, when their clever wordplay and pub rock energy felt perfectly suited to warming up a crowd. Twenty-five years later, I watched them headline Rams Head Live in Baltimore, now seasoned veterans commanding the stage with the same wit but deeper confidence. It's rare to witness that complete arc in your own concert diary — from promising opener to rightful headliner.

social.hook: My first Squeeze show was their opening slot — at a racetrack in Tijuana.
social.caption: In 1987 they opened for Oingo Boingo at Caliente Racetrack. Twenty-five years later I watched them headline Rams Head Live in Baltimore — the full arc, in my own diary.
beats: June 1987: Squeeze opened for Oingo Boingo at a racetrack in Tijuana. Not the most obvious venue for pub rock wordplay.
They were sharp and scrappy — the kind of opener that made you pay attention even before the headliner arrived.
Twenty-five years passed. Then I saw them headline Rams Head Live in Baltimore.
Same wit, deeper confidence. The room was theirs from the first song.
It's rare to hold both ends of an arc like that in your own concert diary — opener to headliner, one band.

posts.headline: Tears For Fears: 37 Years of Shows
posts.prose: I remember discovering Tears For Fears at Pacific Amphitheatre in 1985, when "Songs from the Big Chair" was still fresh and Roland Orzabal's voice felt like it could crack open the world. Four shows across 37 years might not seem like much, but each one marked a different chapter of my life — from that first encounter in Costa Mesa to their triumphant return at the Kia Forum in 2022. What strikes me most is how their pop-rock has aged: the synthesizers that once felt futuristic now carry the weight of memory, and those soaring choruses hit differently when you've lived through four decades of hearing them. Some artists you grow out of; others grow with you.

social.hook: Four shows, 37 years, one band that kept pace with all of it.
social.caption: Four shows across 37 years, and Tears For Fears met me differently every time. The synthesizers that once felt futuristic now carry the weight of memory.
beats: Pacific Amphitheatre, 1985 — 'Songs from the Big Chair' was still fresh, and I had no idea I'd be back.
Four shows over 37 years isn't many. But each one landed at a different chapter of my life.
The synthesizers that felt futuristic then now carry something heavier: four decades of memory.
Those soaring choruses hit differently when you've actually lived through the years between them.
Some artists you grow out of. Others grow with you — and that's the whole point of this archive.

posts.headline: Universal Amphitheater: 5 Shows Over 3 Decades
posts.prose: I remember discovering the Universal Amphitheater through Howard Jones in 1989, drawn by those sweeping synthesizer melodies and his earnest pop optimism. Something about that venue kept pulling me back — the way it nestled into the Hollywood Hills, intimate enough to feel personal but grand enough for proper spectacle. Over 16 years, I caught 5 shows there across three decades, from Siouxsie and the Banshees' dark glamour to The Brian Setzer Orchestra's rockabilly swagger, ending with Tears For Fears in 2005. It became my accidental home base for catching acts that mattered to me, though I didn't realize I was building a pattern until I looked back at the ticket stubs.

social.hook: Universal Amphitheater is gone now. I didn't notice until I counted the stubs.
social.caption: Five shows at Universal Amphitheater across 16 years, starting with Howard Jones in 1989 and ending with Tears for Fears in 2005. I didn't know I had a home base until the venue no longer existed.
beats: Howard Jones in 1989 was my introduction to Universal Amphitheater — synthesizers and Hollywood Hills.
Five shows across 16 years: Howard Jones, Siouxsie and the Banshees, Brian Setzer, Tears for Fears.
Intimate enough to feel personal. Grand enough for spectacle. I kept coming back without planning to.
Tears for Fears in 2005 was the last one. I didn't know that at the time.
Universal Amphitheater is gone. The pattern only became visible once there was nothing left to add to it.

posts.headline: Irvine Meadows: 16 Shows Over 3 Decades
posts.prose: I discovered Irvine Meadows on April 27, 1984, watching Adam Ant command that massive outdoor stage under the California sun. Something about that amphitheater just clicked — the way sound carried across those concrete terraces, how the San Gabriel Mountains framed every performance. Over the next 19 years, I kept coming back, catching everyone from Thompson Twins to Billy Idol to my final show there with Peter Gabriel in 2003. Sixteen concerts spanning three decades at one venue feels almost accidental until you realize it wasn't — some places just become part of your concert DNA.

social.hook: Irvine Meadows kept pulling me back for 19 years — and Adam Ant started it.
social.caption: I found Irvine Meadows on April 27, 1984, watching Adam Ant on that massive outdoor stage. Thirteen artists and 19 years later, Peter Gabriel closed it out.
beats: April 27, 1984: Adam Ant, California sun, and a venue I'd never been to before.
Irvine Meadows had a sound that carried differently — the concrete terraces, the San Gabriels behind every stage.
Thompson Twins. Billy Idol. Depeche Mode. New Order. George Michael. The venue became a pattern I didn't plan.
Peter Gabriel in 2003 was my 16th show there. I didn't know it would be the last.
Some venues end up in your concert DNA. Irvine Meadows got into mine on the very first visit.

posts.headline: Kia Forum: 5 Shows Over 3 Decades
posts.prose: I remember walking into the Forum for the first time in 1990 to see Erasure, that massive bowl of a venue feeling both intimate and overwhelming at 19 years old. Five shows across 33 years have brought me back to Inglewood — from Bell Biv DeVoe's New Jack Swing energy to Elton John's piano grandeur to Tears for Fears' nostalgic pull. My most recent visit was Depeche Mode in 2023, and I realized I've been loyal to this place longer than some of my friendships. There's something about the Forum's acoustics that makes every synthesizer sound like it's coming from the future.

social.hook: The Forum has held five different versions of me, 33 years apart.
social.caption: I was 19 the first time I walked into Kia Forum — Erasure, 1990. Five shows and 33 years later, Depeche Mode closed the loop.
beats: March 1990: 19 years old, Erasure, and the Forum felt like the largest room I'd ever been inside.
Bell Biv DeVoe brought New Jack Swing energy. Elton John filled it with piano grandeur. Different worlds, same bowl.
Tears for Fears made it nostalgic. Depeche Mode in 2023 made it feel like the future.
Five shows. Five artists. I've been coming back to Kia Forum longer than I've known some of my closest friends.
Something in those acoustics makes every synthesizer sound like it hasn't been invented yet.
